title: Unit-cube counting and layered solids
transcript: A solid made of unit cubes can be described by the height of each stack. Add the heights to count cubes, even where a view hides some stacks. If you know only the views, several solids may fit. Maxima tell you how tall at least one stack must be in a row or column.

AMC Upper Primary practice can use unit cubes, layers and silhouettes. Record the counts on a footprint before adding them. Rossmoyne style spatial problems can give two views and ask for the least or greatest possible block count.
A solid block is three cubes wide, three deep and two high. How many unit cubes are inside it altogether? Count the cells of one layer before multiplying by the height.
The footprint is nine positions. There are two equal layers, each filling this footprint. The full block contains eighteen cubes. Cubes in the back and the centre are included.
The heights of six stacks in two rows of three are two, four and three in the first row, and two, five and one in the second. Every stack rests on the floor. Count the cubes in all the stacks.

For every level, count one cube above each footprint cell whose stack reaches it. The level counts are six, five, three, two and one from the floor up. Add those counts, giving seventeen. Adding the six heights directly confirms the same total.

Six nonempty stacks form two rows of three. Looking along the rows, the maximum heights in the three columns are three, six and three. The row maxima in order are six and three. Find the least and greatest possible number of cubes. There are no gaps in any stack.

Every column needs one stack that attains its own maximum. Put those three tall stacks in separate columns. Each of the remaining three stacks must contain at least one cube. Put the tall middle stack in the first row and one of the outer tall stacks in the second row. The row maxima are then satisfied without adding extra cubes.

For the maximum, every stack is capped by both its row and column. Use the smaller of those two limits at every location. That gives three, six, three in the first row and three in every position of the second. Both views still fit, so the maximum is twenty-one cubes.

The maximum seen in a view describes the tallest stack in a line of sight. It does not give that height to all stacks behind it. A maximum model must respect both views. A height allowed by one view may exceed the limit in the other.

Draw the footprint and mark row and column heights. Decide whether you know each stack, or only the maximum over a row or column. For a bound, produce a model that reaches it. Verify all row maxima, all column maxima and the number of cubes.
